newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Belgians snap up heating oil as price rise seen.
newsitem.headline: Belgians snap up heating oil as price rise seen.

text.p: The dramatic rise in oil prices this week and an expected increase in excise duty in October have left Belgians a little more eager than most to fill up their heating oil tanks, traders and analysts say.

Belgium is a relative minnow in the heating oil market with about six percent of European consumption, compared with the German share of 40-45 percent, but traders say increased Belgian demand in September is partly responsible for the rise in heating oil prices and should ensure healthy prices throughout the month.
Sellers in the key Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp market were on Thursday offering heating oil barges at a premium of $5 over underlying IPE gas oil futures, up $3 from Wednesday.
Belgian consumers, among very few in Europe, are cushioned from sudden moves in oil prices as these are fixed by the government.

When the Iraqi crisis sent oil prices soaring at the start of this week, Belgian heating oil consumers, unlike most other European end-users, were able to buy at the previous low prices for two to three days until the government revised its price guideline upwards.
"(Belgian) consumers know that within two to three days, there will be an increase in prices, so they buy," one trader said.

The buying spree at the start of this week would have been short-lived, but for expectations that prices will rise even further. The expectation is that the culprit this time will not be Baghdad or Washington, but their own government.
"There is a strong feeling that excise on heating oil will rise at the start of October," one trader said.
"There is also a rumour that the duty on gasoline at the pump will rise, but the effect in the gas oil market is more noticeable," another trader said.

The excise duty on heating oil, at 210 Belgian francs (or 5.4 Ecus) per 1,000 litres, is significantly lower than the European Union guideline of 18 Ecus. Value-added tax increases the price by a further 21 percent.
A spokeswoman for the Belgian Finance Ministry declined to comment on the speculation about excise increases.
"Nothing has been decided for the budget of 1996 and 1997," she said.
The Belgian budget will be presented on October 1.
